# Results {#sec-results}

```{python}
#| include: false
import pandas as pd
import _helpers as H

bS, gB, gW = H.head("beta_S"), H.head("gamma_B"), H.head("gamma_W")
vd = H.tier1_table("statistic", "capb")
sd2 = H.tier1_value(vd, "two-way SD (country + year effects removed", "capb")
xS = H.tier1_exposure("W_S")
sesoi = H.sesoi()
```

All numbers in this chapter are read at render time from the committed result files (`reports/results/m1_confirmatory.json`, `secondary.json`, `robustness.json`, `exploratory.json`, `predictive.json`); apart from the counts and facts marked as checked, none is typed into the text. Estimates are associations in percentage points (pp) of potential GDP unless stated, and interaction coefficients are per +1 SD of the ageing component. Scheduled elections are predetermined, not exogenous.

## Confirmatory results {#sec-confirmatory}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-headline
#| tbl-cap: "Confirmatory results (V7, N = 715, 27 countries; pp of potential GDP). The family {H1, H2B} is adjusted by Holm; gamma_W is descriptive. Source: reports/results/m1_confirmatory.json."
rows = []
for lab, t in [("H1: $\\beta_S$ (full year of exposure)", bS), ("H2B: $\\gamma_B$ (per SD, between)", gB), ("H2W: $\\gamma_W$ (per SD, within)", gW)]:
    rows.append({
        "Target": lab,
        "Estimate": H.num(t.get("estimate"), 3),
        "95% bootstrap-t interval": H.ival(t.get("ci_lo"), t.get("ci_hi"), 3),
        "p (wild bootstrap)": H.pval(t.get("p_bootstrap"), 4) if t.get("p_bootstrap") is not None else "not tested",
        "p (Holm)": H.pval(t.get("p_holm"), 4) if t.get("p_holm") is not None else "not tested",
        "Pre-registered reading": H.reading_of(t),
    })
H.show_table(pd.DataFrame(rows), widths=[34, 10, 22, 14, 12, 22])
```

@tbl-headline reports the pre-registered analysis, run once after the tag was public. The association of a full year of pre-election exposure to a scheduled election with the CAPB is `{python} H.num(bS.get("estimate"), 3)` pp (95% interval `{python} H.ival(bS.get("ci_lo"), bS.get("ci_hi"), 3)`; wild-bootstrap $p$ = `{python} H.pval(bS.get("p_bootstrap"), 4)`, Holm-adjusted $p$ = `{python} H.pval(bS.get("p_holm"), 4)`). By the pre-registered rule the interval excludes zero, and it is not contained in the equivalence band of ±`{python} H.num(sesoi, 1)` pp: its lower end lies `{python} H.num(abs(bS.get("ci_lo", 0)) - sesoi, 2)` pp beyond the band, so the data are compatible both with associations as small as `{python} H.num(abs(bS.get("ci_hi", 0)), 2)` pp and with associations larger than the SESOI. The criterion pre-registered for H1 (interval excluding zero with Holm-adjusted $p < 0.05$) is `{python} "met" if (bS.get("excludes_zero") and (bS.get("p_holm") or 1) < 0.05) else "not met"`; we return in @sec-robustness and in the Discussion to how much weight this deserves.

For scale: the estimate is about `{python} H.num(abs(bS.get("estimate", 0)) / sd2 if sd2 else None, 2)` of the two-way standard deviation of the CAPB (`{python} H.num(sd2, 2)` pp). Because the maximum observed exposure is `{python} H.num(xS.get("max"), 2)` and a typical exposed country-year has an exposure of about `{python} H.num(xS.get("mean_pos"), 2)`, the implied association for a typical exposed country-year is about `{python} H.num((bS.get("estimate") or 0) * (xS.get("mean_pos") or 0), 2)` pp. The CR1 standard errors, shown for transparency only because they are not valid for this estimator, give $p$ = `{python} H.pval(bS.get("cr1_p"), 4)` for $\beta_S$; the bootstrap $p$-value is the larger of the two, as expected.

For H2B, the association with the between-country ageing component is `{python} H.num(gB.get("estimate"), 3)` pp per standard deviation, with interval `{python} H.ival(gB.get("ci_lo"), gB.get("ci_hi"), 3)`. The interval does not exclude zero (Holm-adjusted $p$ = `{python} H.pval(gB.get("p_holm"), 4)`) and lies inside ±`{python} H.num(sesoi, 1)` pp, so the reading is "equivalent within the SESOI" in the headline specification: the data do not support a between-country ageing heterogeneity of the size that the SESOI defines as relevant. That reading is itself fragile: the interval for $\gamma_B$ lies inside the band in `{python} H.cnt(*H.rob_count("A", "gamma_B", "within_sesoi"))` of the inference sensitivities (@sec-rob-inference). The positive sign means that older countries show a weaker association, but no direction was pre-registered and this is a cross-country contrast. For H2W, the estimate is `{python} H.num(gW.get("estimate"), 3)` pp per standard deviation with interval `{python} H.ival(gW.get("ci_lo"), gW.get("ci_hi"), 3)`: the interval is about `{python} H.num((gW.get("ci_hi") or 0) - (gW.get("ci_lo") or 0), 1)` pp wide, and the estimate is uninformative, as the power analysis anticipated.

```{python}
#| output: asis
H.figure("fig-headline", "f1_headline_estimates.png",
         "Headline estimates and 95% bootstrap-t intervals for beta_S, gamma_B and gamma_W (V7; pp of potential GDP), with the SESOI band. Source: AMECO Spring 2026; Eurostat; ETAD; ParlGov; author's calculations.",
         width="95%")
```

@fig-headline shows the three estimates against the equivalence band. The wide interval of $\gamma_W$ and the interval of $\beta_S$ that straddles the lower edge of the band are the visual summary of the chapter: the evidence is informative about the sign of $\beta_S$, whose statistical support depends on the inference method (@sec-robustness), and, in the headline specification only, about the smallness of $\gamma_B$; it says little else.

```{python}
#| output: asis
H.figure("fig-profile", "f2_election_window_profile.png",
         "Raw mean CAPB (panel A, relative to the country mean) and year-on-year change in the CAPB (panel B) by year relative to a scheduled election, with 95% country-clustered intervals; descriptive, unadjusted, no test. Source: AMECO Spring 2026; ETAD; ParlGov; author's calculations.",
         width="75%")
```

@fig-profile is a descriptive complement that carries no test: raw means by year relative to a scheduled election, without year effects or controls and with overlapping windows for elections that are close together. Its role is to show the raw pattern around scheduled elections; it cannot rule out that the regression association reflects particular years or countries (the leave-one-country-out fits of @sec-rob-sample address that for countries), and it provides no independent evidence.

```{python}
#| output: asis
H.figure("fig-partial", "f3_exposure_vs_capb_partial.png",
         "Partial association of the CAPB with pre-election exposure W^S (Frisch-Waugh residuals after country and year effects and the other M1 regressors; OLS fixed-effects slope; descriptive). Source: AMECO Spring 2026; Eurostat; ETAD; ParlGov; author's calculations.",
         width="75%")
```

@fig-partial displays the same association as a residual scatter. The slope drawn is the OLS fixed-effects coefficient, which differs slightly from the V7 estimate because V7 weights and AR(1)-corrects; the dispersion of the points around the slope is large relative to the slope, which is why the association is imprecisely estimated.

## Robustness and inference sensitivity {#sec-robustness}

The robustness suite was specified after the confirmatory result and before any of its own results were computed (`docs/robustness_spec.md`). It has four groups (A: inference sensitivities to cross-country dependence; B: pre-registered diagnostics; C: sample variants; D: definition variants), and all specifications are reported, without selecting or ranking among them.

```{python}
#| include: false
groups = [("A", "A. Inference sensitivities"), ("C", "C. Sample variants (excl. leave-one-out)"), ("C-LOCO", "C. Leave-one-country-out fits"), ("D", "D. Definition variants"), ("all", "All specifications")]
srows = []
for g, lab in groups:
    kb, nb = H.rob_count(g, "beta_S", "excludes_zero")
    ks, _ = H.rob_count(g, "beta_S", "keeps_sign")
    kg, ng = H.rob_count(g, "gamma_B", "excludes_zero")
    kge, _ = H.rob_count(g, "gamma_B", "within_sesoi")
    srows.append({"Group": lab, "Specifications": nb if nb is not None else H.NA,
                  "$\\beta_S$ keeps sign": H.cnt(ks, nb), "$\\beta_S$ interval excludes 0": H.cnt(kb, nb),
                  "$\\gamma_B$ interval excludes 0": H.cnt(kg, ng), "$\\gamma_B$ interval inside $\\pm$SESOI": H.cnt(kge, ng)})
sumdf = pd.DataFrame(srows)
rowsA, rowsC, rowsD = H.rob_rows("A"), [r for r in H.rob_rows("C") if not r["id"].startswith("C4-loco")], H.rob_rows("D")
rowsL = [r for r in H.rob_rows("C") if r["id"].startswith("C4-loco")]
kA, nA = H.rob_count("A", "beta_S", "excludes_zero")
kC, nC = H.rob_count("C", "beta_S", "excludes_zero")
kL, nL = H.rob_count("C-LOCO", "beta_S", "excludes_zero")
kD, nD = H.rob_count("D", "beta_S", "excludes_zero")
kAll, nAll = H.rob_count("all", "beta_S", "excludes_zero")
sAll, _ = H.rob_count("all", "beta_S", "keeps_sign")
v7A = [r for r in rowsA if r["label"].startswith("V7")]
olsA = [r for r in rowsA if not r["label"].startswith("V7")]
k7 = sum(1 for r in v7A if r["targets"]["beta_S"].get("excludes_zero"))
kO = sum(1 for r in olsA if r["targets"]["beta_S"].get("excludes_zero"))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rob-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Counts of robustness specifications by group (descriptive; specifications share one panel, many are nested, and several rows are one estimate under different inference). Source: reports/results/robustness.json."
if rowsA or rowsC or rowsD:
    H.show_table(sumdf, widths=[40, 14, 16, 20, 20, 24])
else:
    H.not_yet("robustness summary counts")
```

@tbl-rob-summary summarises the suite. The sign of $\beta_S$ is kept in `{python} H.cnt(sAll, nAll)` specifications. Whether the interval excludes zero is a different matter, and it varies sharply by group: it does so in `{python} H.cnt(kA, nA)` inference variants, `{python} H.cnt(kC, nC)` sample variants, `{python} H.cnt(kD, nD)` definition variants and `{python} H.cnt(kL, nL)` leave-one-country-out fits. The counts are descriptive; they are not a vote and not a probability, because the specifications are not independent.

### Inference sensitivities {#sec-rob-inference}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rob-inference
#| tbl-cap: "Inference sensitivities for beta_S and gamma_B (pp of potential GDP; N = 715). Rows with OLS share the point estimate and differ in the inference method; bootstrap rows give bootstrap-t intervals, others estimate +- t(26) x SE. The bootstrap p-value (null imposed) and the interval (unrestricted) are different constructions, so near the margin they can disagree. Source: reports/results/robustness.json, section A."
if rowsA:
    H.show_table(H.spec_table(rowsA), align="lrrrll", widths=[44, 6, 26, 8, 16, 26])
else:
    H.not_yet("section A (inference sensitivities)")
```

```{python}
#| output: asis
H.figure("fig-inference-ladder", "f4_inference_ladder.png",
         "Association of a full year of pre-election exposure with the CAPB under each inference specification (beta_S, pp of potential GDP; 95% intervals; headline V7 at the top; specifications neither ranked nor selected). Source: AMECO Spring 2026; Eurostat; ETAD; ParlGov; author's calculations.",
         width="85%")
```

@tbl-rob-inference and @fig-inference-ladder show where the headline's exclusion of zero is lost. The `{python} len(olsA)` rows that use the OLS fixed-effects estimator, with CR1, wild-bootstrap, Driscoll--Kraay, two-way or CCE inference, have intervals excluding zero in `{python} H.cnt(kO, len(olsA))` cases; the rows that keep V7 and add CCE augmentation have intervals excluding zero in `{python} H.cnt(k7, len(v7A))` cases (in one of them the wild-bootstrap $p$-value is above 0.05 although the interval just excludes zero<!-- CHECKED-STATIC (2026-10-13 against robustness.json at commit e362ba9; re-check only if the suite is re-run): static remark, re-check against section A -->). The OLS point estimates are of the same sign and about the same size as the headline, but their intervals are wider. The reading therefore turns on the efficiency gain from the pre-registered estimator (weights and AR(1) correction), and on how cross-country dependence is handled in the standard errors, and less on the point estimate. We neither prefer nor dismiss any of these rows; the pre-registered estimator was chosen by a mechanical power rule before any association was estimated, but its wild-bootstrap size under cross-country dependence is the known weak point (@sec-inference).

### Sample and definition variants {#sec-rob-sample}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rob-sample
#| tbl-cap: "Sample and definition variants of the headline (V7, wild-cluster bootstrap-t; pp of potential GDP). The leave-one-country-out fits are summarised in the text and listed in Appendix B. Source: reports/results/robustness.json, sections C and D."
rows_cd = rowsC + rowsD
if rows_cd:
    H.show_table(H.spec_table(rows_cd), align="lrrrll", widths=[44, 6, 26, 8, 16, 26])
else:
    H.not_yet("sections C and D (sample and definition variants)")
```

```{python}
#| include: false
notes = H.rob_section("C").get("notes", {})
loco = notes.get("loco", {})
lb, lg = loco.get("beta_S", {}), loco.get("gamma_B", {})
ext = notes.get("extension_2022", {})
not_excl = []
for r in rowsA + rowsC + rowsD + rowsL:
    t = r["targets"]["beta_S"]
    if not t.get("excludes_zero"):
        not_excl.append(r["label"] if not r["id"].startswith("C4-loco") else "leave out " + r["id"].split("-")[-1])
cond = bool(kC is not None and nC and kC / nC >= 0.5 and kL is not None and nL and kL / nL >= 0.5 and nA and kA is not None and kA / nA < 0.5)
verdict = (
    "Taken together, the sign of the association is kept in every specification run. The exclusion of zero holds in most sample and definition variants "
    "and in nearly all leave-one-country-out fits, but not across estimator and inference choices: it is lost under OLS-based inference that handles "
    "cross-country dependence through the standard errors, so the statistical evidence depends on how cross-country dependence is handled more than on the sample."
    if cond else
    "The pattern of the robustness counts differs from the one assumed when this chapter was drafted; read the counts above rather than this sentence."
)
```

@tbl-rob-sample reports the variants run with the pre-registered estimator. The 2022 extension (`{python} H.num(ext.get("n_obs"), 0)` country-years; five countries without a complete 2022 exposure) and the controls model (703 rows) leave the association and its interval close to the headline. Dropping the crisis years 2008--2012 moves the estimate further from zero, whereas dropping 2020--2021 leaves an interval that narrowly includes zero. The 6-month window gives a larger estimate and the 18-month window a smaller one, with the interval including zero; the calendar-year dummy gives a smaller coefficient with an interval excluding zero (the units differ, because the dummy is a whole-year exposure for any election year). Replacing the moderator by `OLDDEP3` or by median age changes $\beta_S$ little.

The leave-one-country-out fits (B = 999 each) keep the sign in `{python} H.cnt(lb.get("n_same_sign"), loco.get("n_fits"))` fits, and the interval excludes zero in `{python} H.cnt(lb.get("n_interval_excludes_zero"), loco.get("n_fits"))`. The estimate ranges from `{python} H.num(lb.get("min"), 3)` (without `{python} lb.get("argmin", H.NA)`) to `{python} H.num(lb.get("max"), 3)` (without `{python} lb.get("argmax", H.NA)`); the largest shift occurs when `{python} lb.get("most_influential", H.NA)` is removed (`{python} H.num(lb.get("most_influential_shift"), 3)` pp). For $\gamma_B$ the range is `{python} H.num(lg.get("min"), 3)` to `{python} H.num(lg.get("max"), 3)`. No single country accounts for the headline, although the one leave-one-out fit whose interval includes zero (without `{python} ", ".join(r["id"].split("-")[-1] for r in rowsL if not r["targets"]["beta_S"].get("excludes_zero")) or "none"`) shows that the interval is not far from zero.

The specifications whose 95% interval for $\beta_S$ does *not* exclude zero are: `{python} "; ".join(not_excl) if not_excl else "none"`. <!-- CHECKED-STATIC (2026-10-13 against robustness.json at commit e362ba9; re-check only if the suite is re-run): this list is generated at render time; re-read it after any re-run of the robustness suite -->

`{python} verdict` We therefore read the confirmatory result as `{python} H.evidence_core()`. <!-- CHECKED-STATIC (2026-10-13 against robustness.json at commit e362ba9; re-check only if the suite is re-run): the preceding sentence is conditional on the render-time counts; re-check the wording after any re-run -->

### Diagnostics {#sec-rob-diagnostics}

```{python}
#| include: false
B = H.rob_section("B")
mw = B.get("modified_wald", {}).get("v7_residuals", {})
wo = B.get("wooldridge", {})
lp = B.get("lead_placebo", {})
lp20 = B.get("lead_placebo_to_2020", {})
haus = B.get("hausman_mundlak", {})
vif = B.get("vif", {})
cips = B.get("cips_capb_trend", {})
lin_b = B.get("binned_between", {})
lin_w = B.get("binned_within", {})
```

The pre-registered diagnostics describe the data and were not used to choose any specification; their full tables are in [Appendix B](#sec-app-robustness). In brief, the diagnostics are in line with the design choices. Groupwise heteroskedasticity is pronounced (modified Wald statistic for the V7 residuals `{python} H.num(mw.get("statistic"), 0)`, Monte Carlo $p$ = `{python} H.pval(mw.get("p_value_mc"), 4)`), which supports the weighting step. Serial correlation is present (Wooldridge test, $F$ = `{python} H.num(wo.get("f_statistic"), 1)` on (`{python} wo.get("df1", H.NA)`, `{python} wo.get("df2", H.NA)`) degrees of freedom, $p$ = `{python} H.sci(wo.get("p_value"))`), which supports the AR(1) correction. The Mundlak-form Hausman test rejects the null that the country means are irrelevant ($p$ = `{python} H.sci(haus.get("p_value_f"))`), which supports fixed effects. The CIPS panel unit-root test with a trend rejects a unit root for the CAPB at 5% (CIPS = `{python} H.num(cips.get("cips"), 2)`), whereas the lagged old-age dependency ratio cannot reject one, so that the within-country ageing term should be read with this in mind. Variance inflation factors flag the 2016--2021 era interaction (`{python} ", ".join(vif.get("flagged_within", [])) or "none"`); the within-ageing interaction is close to the threshold. Binned estimates give no evidence against linearity of the interactions (linearity $F$-test $p$ = `{python} H.pval(lin_b.get("linearity_p"), 2)` for the between and `{python} H.pval(lin_w.get("linearity_p"), 2)` for the within component), although each bin rests on few countries.

The lead placebo is the diagnostic closest to a test of anticipation. Adding the share of the year inside months 13--24 before a scheduled election gives a lead coefficient of `{python} H.est_ci(lp.get("lead"))` pp ($p$ = `{python} H.pval(lp.get("lead", {}).get("p"), 3)`), and `{python} H.est_ci(lp20.get("lead"))` pp when the sample ends in 2020 (the lead window of 2021 reaches into 2023, where the calendar is incomplete). The lead is indistinguishable from zero, but with an interval wider than the headline interval it cannot rule out associations of the size of $\beta_S$. A placebo of this kind cannot establish the absence of anticipation, and it does not make scheduled elections exogenous [@rambachan2023].

## Secondary outcomes {#sec-secondary}

```{python}
#| include: false
fam = H.sec_outcomes("family")
weaker = {"S1a": -1, "S1b": -1, "S1c": -1, "S1e": -1, "S1d": 1, "S1f-1": 1, "S1f-2": 1, "S1g-1": 1, "S1g-2": 1, "S1g-3": 1}
n_weak = sum(1 for o in fam if weaker.get(o["id"]) and o["targets"]["beta_S"]["estimate"] * weaker[o["id"]] > 0)
n_excl = sum(1 for o in fam if (o["targets"]["beta_S"]["ci_lo"] > 0 or o["targets"]["beta_S"]["ci_hi"] < 0))
hi_rho = [o["id"] for o in fam if (o.get("diagnostics", {}).get("rho_nickell") or 0) >= 0.85]
byid = {o["id"]: o for o in fam}
def b(i): return byid.get(i, {}).get("targets", {}).get("beta_S", {}).get("estimate")
mult = H.SEC.get("multiplicity", {})
bh_ids = [o["id"] for o in fam if o["targets"]["beta_S"].get("bh_reject")]
```

The pre-registration pre-specifies the same model for ten further outcomes (`docs/secondary_spec.md`): balances (headline primary balance, net lending, the change in the CAPB), primary expenditure, revenue, social benefits in cash and in kind, and three COFOG functions (social protection, old age, health). The outcomes other than the change in the CAPB are *not* cyclically adjusted, so a match or a mismatch with the CAPB result mixes policy and cyclical components. Multiplicity is controlled by Benjamini--Hochberg over the ten $\beta_S$ tests; the headline $\beta_S$, $\gamma_B$ and $\gamma_W$ of the CAPB model are reproduced exactly (self-check passed).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-secondary
#| tbl-cap: "beta_S for the ten secondary outcomes (V7 on each outcome's own sample; pp of GDP, except the change in CAPB in pp of potential GDP). BH: Benjamini-Hochberg at q = 0.05 over the ten tests. Source: reports/results/secondary.json."
rows = []
for o in fam:
    t = o["targets"]["beta_S"]
    rows.append({
        "ID": o["id"], "Outcome": o["label"], "N": o["n_obs"],
        "$\\beta_S$ [95% interval]": H.est_ci(t),
        "p": H.pval(t.get("p_bootstrap")), "BH q": H.pval(t.get("q_bh")),
        "BH": "reject" if t.get("bh_reject") else "no",
    })
if rows:
    H.show_table(pd.DataFrame(rows), align="llrrrrl", widths=[7, 40, 6, 28, 8, 8, 8])
else:
    H.not_yet("secondary outcomes")
```

```{python}
#| output: asis
H.figure("fig-secondary", "secondary_forest.png",
         "beta_S for the secondary outcomes with 95% bootstrap-t intervals. Source: AMECO Spring 2026; Eurostat; ETAD; ParlGov; author's calculations.",
         width="90%")
```

@tbl-secondary and @fig-secondary show that the Benjamini--Hochberg adjustment rejects `{python} H.cnt(mult.get("n_bh_reject"), mult.get("n_family"))` outcomes (`{python} ", ".join(bh_ids) or "none"`, the change in the CAPB; the Benjamini--Yekutieli adjustment rejects `{python} H.cnt(mult.get("n_by_reject"), mult.get("n_family"))`). The change in the CAPB is arithmetically related to its level, so this rejection is not independent corroboration of the headline. The unadjusted intervals exclude zero for `{python} n_excl` of ten outcomes. `{python} n_weak` of the ten point estimates are in the direction of a weaker budget (a lower balance, lower revenue or higher spending). The balance outcomes have the same sign as the CAPB result, with smaller point estimates and intervals that include zero for the level of the headline primary balance and of net lending: `{python} H.num(b("S1a"), 2)` and `{python} H.num(b("S1b"), 2)` pp of GDP, against `{python} H.num(bS.get("estimate"), 2)` for the CAPB. The change in the CAPB has an association of `{python} H.num(b("S1c"), 2)` pp of potential GDP, a different quantity that is not directly comparable in size. On the composition side, $\beta_S$ is `{python} H.num(b("S1d"), 2, True)` pp of GDP for primary expenditure and `{python} H.num(b("S1e"), 2)` pp for revenue; the difference of the two, `{python} H.num((b("S1e") or 0) - (b("S1d") or 0), 2)` pp, is arithmetic on two separate fits and not a decomposition of the balance. No spending or revenue component clearly accounts for the CAPB association: the intervals for primary expenditure and revenue include zero, and the one component whose interval excludes zero before adjustment, social protection spending (COFOG GF10), has the opposite sign to a pre-election expansion.

A caution applies to the persistence of the spending-share series: `{python} ", ".join(hi_rho) or "no outcome"` have a Nickell-corrected persistence of at least 0.85, where the AR(1) correction and the bootstrap were not validated (the pre-registered power study used a persistence of about 0.7). Those intervals deserve less weight. The $\gamma_B$ and $\gamma_W$ estimates for the secondary outcomes are descriptive and are in `reports/results/secondary.md`.

## Early elections and the post-election window {#sec-early}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-early
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive terms from the headline CAPB fit (no test, no multiplicity adjustment; pp of potential GDP). Early elections are endogenous. Source: reports/results/secondary.json, S3."
s3 = H.SEC.get("s3", {}).get("targets", {})
rows = []
for k, lab in [("beta_E", "$\\beta_E$: early-election exposure $W^E$"), ("beta_U", "$\\beta_U$: unclassified-election exposure $W^U$"), ("rho_Post", "$\\rho_P$: share of the year within 12 months after any election")]:
    if k in s3:
        rows.append({"Term": lab, "Estimate [95% bootstrap-t interval]": H.est_ci(s3[k], 3)})
if rows:
    H.show_table(pd.DataFrame(rows), widths=[54, 36])
else:
    H.not_yet("the early-election terms (S3)")
```

@tbl-early reports, descriptively, the other election terms of M1. Early elections are chosen strategically and respond to fiscal and economic conditions, so these coefficients carry no causal reading and no test. The early-election term `{python} H.est_ci(s3.get("beta_E"), 2)` is negative with an interval that includes zero and is imprecise; it is of the same sign as $\beta_S$ and cannot be distinguished from it or from zero. This is not in contradiction with the finding of @afonso2026 that spending rises around regular but not early elections, because their outcome is expenditure growth and ours is the CAPB level. The unclassified-election term is estimated on very few country-years and is uninformative. The post-election term `{python} H.est_ci(s3.get("rho_Post"), 2)` is negative, with an interval that excludes zero. Because it is not part of any family and is not adjusted for multiplicity, we do not interpret it beyond noting its implication for the reading of $\beta_S$: the reference group for $\beta_S$ is country-years outside both the pre- and the post-election windows, so a general deterioration of the CAPB around elections, before and after, is compatible with both coefficients.

The pre-registration (section 11) lists analyses that were deliberately kept outside the confirmatory and secondary families, and `docs/exploratory_spec.md` fixed their details on 2026-10-13, after the confirmatory, secondary and robustness results were known and before any exploratory result existed. They are labelled *exploratory* for three reasons: they were specified after the author had seen the headline estimates; their moderators (a de jure fiscal-rule index, debt and accession splits, a euro indicator) were not part of the frozen design; and the family below was fixed by hand rather than by a pre-registered rule. All use the pre-registered estimator V7 (feasible WLS with AR(1) GLS) and wild-cluster bootstrap-t inference with B = `{python} f'{H.EXP.get("n_boot", 0):,}'`, add one interaction with $W^S$ to the M1 design per model, and are associations only. Seven coefficients form the exploratory family: the rule-strength interaction (E1), its triple interaction with between-country ageing (E2), a hinge in the between-ageing interaction (E3), and four group differences in the $W^S$ association by debt (E4a between countries, E4b within years), EU accession cohort (E4c) and euro membership (E4d). Multiplicity is controlled by the Benjamini--Hochberg procedure at $q = 0.05$ over these seven $p$-values, with the Benjamini--Yekutieli adjustment beside it. No equivalence reading against the SESOI is applied, because the SESOI of `{python} H.num(sesoi, 1)` pp was set for $\beta_S$ only; the minimum detectable effect (MDE) is shown next to every interval instead.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-exploratory
#| tbl-cap: "Exploratory family of seven coefficients (V7; pp of potential GDP per +1 SD of the moderator, or difference between two groups; 95% bootstrap-t intervals). Raw p: null-imposed wild-cluster bootstrap-t, unadjusted; q: Benjamini-Hochberg over the seven. MDE: effect detectable with 80% power at the estimated persistence, from the wild bootstrap for E1 and E2 and, marked with an asterisk, the size-adjusted CR1 value for E3 and E4 (indicative only). Source: reports/results/exploratory.json."
rows = []
short = {"E1": "$\\gamma_F$: $W^S$ x rule index (2016-2021)", "E2": "$\\delta_{BF}$: $W^S$ x ageing x rule index", "E3": "$\\delta_H$: ageing hinge at the median",
         "E4a": "High- minus low-debt country", "E4b": "Debt above vs below year median", "E4c": "Accession member minus EU-14", "E4d": "Euro minus non-euro"}
for r in xr:
    mv, wild = H.exp_mde(r)
    rows.append({"Model": r["model"], "Coefficient": short.get(r["model"], r["target"]), "N": r["n_obs"],
                 "Estimate [95% interval]": H.est_ci(r), "Raw p": H.pval(r.get("p_bootstrap")), "BH q": H.pval(r.get("q_bh")),
                 "MDE": H.num(mv, 2) + ("" if wild else "*")})
if rows:
    H.show_table(pd.DataFrame(rows), align="llrrrrr", widths=[6, 40, 6, 28, 8, 8, 8])
else:
    H.not_yet("the exploratory family")
```

```{python}
         "Exploratory coefficients with 95% bootstrap-t intervals (V7; wild-cluster, B = 9,999; unit per row as stated). No coefficient is rejected by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure over the seven. Associations only. Source: AMECO Spring 2026; Fiscal Governance Database 2025 update; Eurostat; author's calculations.",
         width="90%")
```

@tbl-exploratory and @fig-exploratory give the family. The Benjamini--Hochberg procedure rejects `{python} H.cnt(xm.get("n_bh_reject"), xm.get("m_used"))` coefficients and the Benjamini--Yekutieli procedure `{python} H.cnt(xm.get("n_by_reject"), xm.get("m_used"))`; the smallest raw $p$-value is `{python} H.pval(min_p)`. The intervals are wide, and the MDE exceeds the project's not-powered line of 1.0 pp for `{python} H.cnt(n_gt1, len(mdes))` coefficients. The correct reading is therefore not that moderation is absent but that the design cannot detect heterogeneity of the size that would matter for the headline: the intervals are compatible with no moderation and with moderation as large as, or larger than, $\beta_S$ itself.

The group difference between accession members and the EU-14 (E4c) is the only coefficient whose interval excludes zero before adjustment: `{python} H.est_ci(xby.get("E4c"), 2)`, raw $p$ = `{python} H.pval(xby.get("E4c", {}).get("p_bootstrap"))`, BH $q$ = `{python} H.pval(xby.get("E4c", {}).get("q_bh"))`. We treat it as a nominal pattern and not as a finding. It is one of seven post hoc contrasts, the null-imposed $p$-value does not reach 0.05, the interval just excludes zero, and the contrast compares 13 accession members with 14 older members, so that it is confounded with every other difference between the two groups (income, institutions, period of membership). For description only, the group-specific associations are `{python} H.est_ci(e4c.get("beta_S_D1"), 2)` for accession members and `{python} H.est_ci(e4c.get("beta_S_D0"), 2)` for the EU-14.

**E1: fiscal-rule moderation.** The moderator is the lagged de jure design-strength score of national numerical fiscal rules (raw C-FRSI of the Fiscal Governance Database, 2025 update), which measures the design of rules and not their enforcement or compliance, and is retroactively revised by its producer. The index has gaps in the early 2010s (and for one country until 2016), so E1 uses 2016--2021 with N = `{python} xav.get("e1_rows")` country-years in `{python} xav.get("e1_countries")` countries, of which `{python} xav.get("e1_ws_positive_rows")` carry positive exposure; the within-country variation of the index rests on `{python} H.fact("e1_changes")` year-to-year changes. The coefficient per +1 SD of the index is `{python} H.est_ci(xby.get("E1"), 2)`; the feasible-WLS-only and OLS versions give `{python} H.est_ci(e1ladder.get("V3"), 2)` and `{python} H.est_ci(e1ladder.get("V0"), 2)`, and leaving out each country in turn gives estimates from `{python} H.num(min(f["estimate"] for f in e1l), 2)` to `{python} H.num(max(f["estimate"] for f in e1l), 2)` with the interval excluding zero in `{python} H.cnt(e1.get("loo", {}).get("n_exclude_zero_changes"), len(e1l))` fits (the fit without `{python} e1.get("loo", {}).get("most_influential", H.NA)`). The sign is not stable across sensitivities: the estimate is `{python} H.num(e1sens.get("noage", {}).get("targets", {}).get("gamma_F", {}).get("estimate"), 2)` without the ageing interactions and `{python} H.num(e1sens.get("window_2012_2021", {}).get("targets", {}).get("gamma_F", {}).get("estimate"), 2)` in the longer 2012--2021 window (which uses back-cast index values). The pre-registered promotion check asked whether E1 could return to the secondary family: its wild-bootstrap MDE would have to be at most `{python} H.num(xpc.get("lines_pp", {}).get("promotion"), 1)` pp per SD. It is `{python} H.num(xpc.get("V7", {}).get("wcb_mde_pp_per_sd_rho_hat"), 2)` pp (`{python} H.num(xpc.get("V7", {}).get("wcb_mde_pp_per_sd_rho0"), 2)` pp at zero persistence) for V7, and similar for the two alternatives, so the check fails and E1 stays exploratory. The E2 triple interaction (`{python} H.est_ci(xby.get("E2"), 2)`) was flagged as severely underpowered in advance and is an indication of how wide the uncertainty is, not a test.

**E3: nonlinear ageing.** With a knot at the median of the between-country component, the change in the slope above the knot is `{python} H.est_ci(xby.get("E3"), 2)`; the descriptive slopes below and above the knot are `{python} H.est_ci(e3.get("slope_below"), 2)` and `{python} H.est_ci(e3.get("slope_above"), 2)`. The between component has 27 distinct values, and no departure from the linear ageing interaction can be established.

**E6: country typology.** A $k$-means clustering of the 27 countries on five standardised country-level features (mean lagged debt, interest, CAPB, interquartile range of the CAPB, and old-age dependency) is descriptive only: it uses the outcome, carries no inference on membership, and its labels are not used in any model. The admissible partition with the highest silhouette has $k$ = `{python} e6.get("chosen_k")`, with a mean silhouette of `{python} H.num(e6.get("silhouette"), 2)`, which is weak structure on the Kaufman--Rousseeuw scale. It separates `{python} ", ".join(mem.get("2", []))` (mean debt `{python} H.num(cm.get("2", {}).get("mean_debt"), 0)`% of GDP, against `{python} H.num(cm.get("1", {}).get("mean_debt"), 0)`% for the other `{python} len(mem.get("1", []))`) from the rest. The partition is not stable under the clustering algorithm's starting values: only `{python} H.pct(stab.get("share_equal_to_reference"))` of `{python} stab.get("n_seeds")` single-start runs reproduce the reference partition (median adjusted Rand index `{python} H.num(stab.get("ari_median"), 2)`), although a Ward-linkage cut gives the identical partition (adjusted Rand index `{python} H.num(stab.get("ari_ward_vs_reference"), 2)`). We read it as a description of three high-debt, high-interest countries against the rest, not as a typology.

**Not run.** `{python} "; ".join(f"{k}: {v}" for k, v in H.EXP.get("not_run", {}).items())`. The thesis therefore says nothing about E5, about the researcher's optional extension (E7, not chosen) or about heterogeneity by democratic age.

## Predictive evaluation {#sec-predictive}

```{python}

pr = H.pred_res()
pyears = pr.get("P", {}).get("years", [])
hyears = pr.get("H", {}).get("years", [])
p0 = H.pacc("P", "P0")
fam6 = H.pfam()
sched = H.PRED.get("meta", {}).get("schedule_agreement", {})
sd50, sd80 = H.pred_power_sd()
gain = H.pred_oracle_gain()
loco = pr.get("loco", {}).get("accuracy", {})
loco_main = [v.get("ratio_to_main") for v in loco.values() if v.get("ratio_to_main") is not None] or [None]
cl4 = [H.pacc("P", m) for m in ("P1a-B1", "P1a-B2", "P1b-B1", "P1b-B2")]
r4 = [c.get("ratio") for c in cl4 if c.get("ratio") is not None] or [None]
all_contain_one = bool(cl4) and all(c.get("ratio_ci") and c["ratio_ci"][0] <= 1 <= c["ratio_ci"][1] for c in cl4)
hr4 = [H.pacc("H", m).get("ratio") for m in ("P1a-B1", "P1a-B2", "P1b-B1", "P1b-B2") if H.pacc("H", m).get("ratio") is not None] or [None]
holm_all_one = bool(fam6) and all((r.get("p_holm") or 0) >= 0.9999 for r in fam6.values())
rmin_raw = min((r["p"] for r in fam6.values()), default=None)
pol_a, pol_b = H.pimp("P1a", "group:political"), H.pimp("P1b", "group:political")
fm_a, fm_b = H.pimp("P1a", "group:fiscal_macro"), H.pimp("P1b", "group:fiscal_macro")
dem_a, dem_b = H.pimp("P1a", "group:demographic"), H.pimp("P1b", "group:demographic")
inc_a, inc_b = fam6.get("P1a: B2 vs B1", {}), fam6.get("P1b: B2 vs B1", {})
```

This section is a predictive and non-causal exercise, separate from the confirmatory question (@sec-strategy-predictive). Its specification (`docs/predictive_spec.md`) was fixed before any forecast was computed, and all numbers are read from `reports/results/predictive.json`.

*Target and design.* The target is the next-year change in the CAPB, $y_{i,T} = \text{CAPB}_{i,T+1} - \text{CAPB}_{i,T}$, in pp of potential GDP, for the `{python} len(pr.get("codes", []))` member states. Forecasts are one-step-ahead from an expanding window: at origin $T$ (the end of year $T$) every model is refitted from scratch on all complete rows with forecast year up to $T$, hyperparameters are chosen by time-ordered validation inside the training window, and the next-year change is forecast for each country. The primary block P has origins `{python} (pyears[0] - 1) if pyears else H.NA`--`{python} (pyears[-1] - 1) if pyears else H.NA`, forecast years `{python} pyears[0] if pyears else H.NA`--`{python} pyears[-1] if pyears else H.NA` and `{python} p0.get("n", H.NA)` forecasts; block H (forecast years `{python} hyears[0] if hyears else H.NA`--`{python} hyears[-1] if hyears else H.NA`, `{python} H.pacc("H", "P0").get("n", H.NA)` forecasts) is reported descriptively and never pooled with P. The benchmark is persistence (a forecast of no change, P0). The learned models are ridge or elastic-net regression (P1a) and gradient-boosted trees (scikit-learn histogram boosting, P1b), each on two feature sets: B1 holds the lagged CAPB level and last change, debt, the output gap, the interest--growth differential and euro membership; B2 adds four election-calendar columns and three demographic measures. The incremental value of the political and demographic block is the comparison of B2 with B1 within a model class.

*Information set.* Every feature is dated on or before the origin; country means and standardisation use the training window only, and no function of the calendar year enters. The election calendar is built from the statutory schedule only: known pre- and post-election exposure of the forecast year and of the origin year from elections already held plus the next scheduled date (date of the last election plus its term length). The realised class or date of any later election is never used, so early elections are unforecastable by construction. This rule agrees with ETAD's recorded scheduled date within `{python} sched.get("tolerance_days", H.NA)` days for `{python} H.pct(sched.get("share_within_tolerance"), 1)` of `{python} sched.get("n_pairs", H.NA)` comparable elections, so it measures the schedule with error but without look-ahead. Accuracy is the root mean squared error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) in pp of potential GDP, with 95% country-cluster bootstrap intervals (27 clusters, B = 9,999). Models are compared with the Diebold--Mariano test with the Harvey--Leybourne--Newbold correction on the `{python} len(pyears)` yearly cross-country mean squared-loss differentials (Student $t$, `{python} len(pyears) - 1` degrees of freedom); the six pre-listed comparisons (four models against persistence, and B2 against B1 for each class) form a family adjusted by Holm's procedure.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-pred-accuracy
#| tbl-cap: "Out-of-sample accuracy, block P (351 forecasts; pp of potential GDP). Ratio: RMSE relative to persistence P0, with 95% country-cluster bootstrap interval. P0b repeats the last change. Source: reports/results/predictive.json."
names = [("P0", "Persistence (P0)"), ("P0b", "Last change repeated (P0b)"), ("P1a-B1", "Ridge / elastic net, B1"), ("P1a-B2", "Ridge / elastic net, B2"),
         ("P1b-B1", "Gradient-boosted trees, B1"), ("P1b-B2", "Gradient-boosted trees, B2")]
rows = []
for k, lab in names:
    a = H.pacc("P", k)
    if not a:
        continue
    rows.append({"Model": lab, "RMSE [95% interval]": f'{H.num(a.get("rmse"), 2)} {H.ival(*(a.get("rmse_ci") or [None, None]), 2)}',
                 "MAE": H.num(a.get("mae"), 2),
                 "RMSE ratio to P0 [95% interval]": "1 (benchmark)" if k == "P0" else f'{H.num(a.get("ratio"), 3)} {H.ival(*(a.get("ratio_ci") or [None, None]), 3)}'})
if rows:
    H.show_table(pd.DataFrame(rows), align="lrrr", widths=[34, 26, 8, 30])
else:
    H.not_yet("the predictive accuracy table")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-pred-dm
#| tbl-cap: "Diebold-Mariano comparisons (Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold correction, 13 yearly loss differentials, two-sided; Holm over the six). Mean loss difference in pp squared, positive when the first-named model is better. Relative MSE reduction with 95% country-cluster bootstrap interval. Source: reports/results/predictive.json."
lab6 = {"P1a-B1 vs P0": "Ridge / elastic net B1 against persistence", "P1b-B1 vs P0": "Trees B1 against persistence",
        "P1a-B2 vs P0": "Ridge / elastic net B2 against persistence", "P1b-B2 vs P0": "Trees B2 against persistence",
        "P1a: B2 vs B1": "Ridge / elastic net: B2 against B1", "P1b: B2 vs B1": "Trees: B2 against B1"}
rows = []
for k, lab in lab6.items():
    r = fam6.get(k)
    if not r:
        continue
    lo, hi = r.get("rel_reduction_ci") or [None, None]
    rows.append({"Comparison": lab, "Mean loss difference": H.num(r.get("mean"), 3), "HLN statistic": H.num(r.get("hln"), 2),
                 "Raw p": H.pval(r.get("p"), 3), "Holm p": H.pval(r.get("p_holm"), 3),
                 "Relative MSE reduction, % [95% interval]": f'{H.num(100 * r["rel_reduction"], 1)} {H.ival(None if lo is None else 100 * lo, None if hi is None else 100 * hi, 1)}'})
if rows:
    H.show_table(pd.DataFrame(rows), align="lrrrrr", widths=[40, 12, 10, 8, 8, 28])
else:
    H.not_yet("the Diebold-Mariano comparisons")
```

@tbl-pred-accuracy gives the accuracy of the main models. Persistence has an RMSE of `{python} H.num(p0.get("rmse"), 2)` pp; the four learned models have RMSE ratios to persistence of `{python} H.num(min(r4), 3)` to `{python} H.num(max(r4), 3)`, and `{python} "every one of their intervals contains one" if all_contain_one else "not every interval contains one (see the table)"`. Repeating the last change (P0b) is clearly worse than persistence (ratio `{python} H.num(H.pacc("P", "P0b").get("ratio"), 2)`). @tbl-pred-dm gives the six Holm-adjusted comparisons: the smallest raw $p$-value is `{python} H.pval(rmin_raw, 2)` and `{python} "all six Holm-adjusted p-values equal 1" if holm_all_one else "the Holm-adjusted p-values are shown in the table"`. No model is distinguishable from persistence. Errors are dominated by the crisis years and by country-specific episodes, as @fig-pred-errors shows, and the learned models follow persistence closely in most years.

```{python}
#| output: asis
H.figure("fig-pred-errors", "predictive_errors.png",
         "Out-of-sample RMSE by forecast year (panel A) and RMSE ratio to persistence with 95% country-cluster intervals for block P and, as indicative only, block H (panel B). Predictive and non-causal. Source: European Commission AMECO Spring 2026, Eurostat, ETAD v1.0.0 and ParlGov 2024; author's calculations.",
         width="95%")
```

*Incremental value of the political and demographic block.* Comparing B2 with B1 within a model class, the relative reduction of the mean squared error is `{python} H.num(100 * inc_a.get("rel_reduction", float("nan")), 1)`% for ridge / elastic net (raw $p$ = `{python} H.pval(inc_a.get("p"), 2)`) and `{python} H.num(100 * inc_b.get("rel_reduction", float("nan")), 1)`% for trees (raw $p$ = `{python} H.pval(inc_b.get("p"), 2)`), where a negative value means that the larger set is slightly worse; both Holm-adjusted $p$-values are `{python} H.pval(inc_a.get("p_holm"), 2)`. There is therefore no evidence that the political and demographic block improves out-of-sample prediction of the next-year change in the CAPB, and for trees the point estimate is slightly worse with it. The statement has limited reach. With `{python} len(pyears)` forecast years the test can detect only a mean loss differential of about `{python} sd50` standard deviations of the yearly differential with 50% power and `{python} sd80` with 80% power, so a small gain would not be detected; and the null is about prediction from a statutory calendar and slow-moving demography, not about whether elections matter for fiscal policy, so it neither supports nor contradicts the association of @sec-confirmatory.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-pred-importance
#| tbl-cap: "Out-of-sample permutation importance by feature group, origins 2008-2020: increase in squared error (%) when the group is permuted jointly across countries within a year, pooled, with 95% country-cluster bootstrap interval. Predictive description only. Source: reports/results/predictive.json."
def imp(t):
    ci = t.get("ci") or [None, None]
    return f'{H.num(t.get("pooled_pct"), 2)} {H.ival(ci[0], ci[1], 2)}' if t else H.NA
rows = [{"Feature group": "Lagged fiscal and macro", "Ridge / elastic net, B2": imp(fm_a), "Trees, B2": imp(fm_b)},
        {"Feature group": "Political (election calendar)", "Ridge / elastic net, B2": imp(pol_a), "Trees, B2": imp(pol_b)},
        {"Feature group": "Demographic", "Ridge / elastic net, B2": imp(dem_a), "Trees, B2": imp(dem_b)}]
if fm_a:
    H.show_table(pd.DataFrame(rows), align="lrr", widths=[34, 28, 28])
else:
    H.not_yet("the permutation importance")
```

*Importance.* SHAP values were not computed (the package is not installed); out-of-sample permutation importance and accumulated local effects (ALE) are used instead. @tbl-pred-importance shows that the usable signal sits in the lagged fiscal and macro group: permuting it raises the squared error by `{python} H.num(fm_a.get("pooled_pct"), 1)`% (ridge / elastic net) and `{python} H.num(fm_b.get("pooled_pct"), 1)`% (trees), with intervals above zero, whereas permuting the political group changes it by `{python} H.num(pol_a.get("pooled_pct"), 2)`% and `{python} H.num(pol_b.get("pooled_pct"), 2)`% with intervals containing zero. The ALE curves in @fig-pred-importance show mean reversion in the CAPB level and a mildly positive slope in debt, and a flat curve for the known pre-election exposure. Importance describes which inputs a forecast relies on, not what produces the outcome.

```{python}
#| output: asis
H.figure("fig-pred-importance", "predictive_importance.png",
         "Grouped permutation importance (panel A) and first-order accumulated local effects of selected features for the model refitted at origin 2020 (panel B). Predictive description, not causal. Source: European Commission AMECO Spring 2026, Eurostat, ETAD v1.0.0 and ParlGov 2024; author's calculations.",
         width="95%")
```

*Block H, oracle diagnostics and country transfer.* In block H (forecast years `{python} hyears[0] if hyears else H.NA`--`{python} hyears[-1] if hyears else H.NA`) the four learned models have RMSE ratios to persistence of `{python} H.num(min(hr4), 2)` to `{python} H.num(max(hr4), 2)`. This is descriptive only: two forecast years support no inference, the intervals in @fig-pred-errors are indicative, and block H is not pristine, because the 2022 CAPB entered the robustness extension of @sec-robustness (2023 did not). It should not be read as a confirmation. Oracle diagnostics replace the statutory calendar with ETAD's ex-post scheduled dates or add the realised exposure of the forecast year; they leak the future by construction and are not forecasts. The best of them lowers RMSE by `{python} H.num(gain, 1)`% relative to the strict set, never more than 1%, so the strict calendar rule does not hide a gain that leaked information would reveal; the political columns carry little signal either way. In leave-one-country-out refits, which remove each country from fitting, standardisation and validation, the RMSE is `{python} H.num(min(loco_main), 3)` to `{python} H.num(max(loco_main), 3)` times that of the main run, so the models transfer to an unseen country about as well as they predict within the sample, which is close to persistence.

*What is not claimed.* The exercise is not real-time forecasting: the target and all features are the Spring 2026 vintage of the CAPB and the output gap, which are model estimates revised with later data, so accuracy levels are not operational forecast skill (the revisions are described in [Appendix E](#sec-app-revisions)). The election columns measure the statutory schedule with error and cannot see early elections. The results are associations between predictors and an outcome, never causal; a predictor that improves accuracy would still be only a predictor, and the null for the political block is not evidence that elections do not matter. The one deviation of the predictive specification that matters for reading (its quoted 71% schedule agreement divided by all calendar rows and was corrected to the value above) is recorded in `reports/results/predictive.md`; it changes no model or test.
